a.entradas.nergal.titulo_alternativo: Nergal/Erra, the one who unleashed the nuclear weapons
a.entradas.nergal.interpretacion: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), Sitchin identifies Erra with Nergal and presents him as the Anunnaki who, together with Ninurta, used the "weapons of terror" against the Sinai spaceport and the cities of the plain in 2024 BC.
a.entradas.nergal.afirmaciones.0.replica: Nergal is the god of the Underworld, plague and war, and Erra shares these traits with him. The Poem of Erra and Ishum dates to the 1st millennium BC, and its "weapons" are the Seven demons and personified plague.
a.entradas.nergal.afirmaciones.0.fuente_: L. Cagni, The Poem of Erra, 1977; Black and Green, 1992
a.entradas.nergal.veredicto: Nergal is the lord of the Underworld and of plague; his nuclear role is a modern reading of a metaphorical poem.
a.entradas.ninurta.titulo_alternativo: Ninurta, the warrior of the flying machines
a.entradas.ninurta.interpretacion: Sitchin presents Ninurta, son of Enlil, as the military commander of the Anunnaki: the one who recovers the Tablet of Destinies stolen by Anzu in an aerial battle, who storms the Great Pyramid in the "pyramid wars" (Lugal-e) and who accompanies Nergal in the nuclear attack of 2024 BC. His "divine bird" would be an aircraft.
a.entradas.ninurta.afirmaciones.0.afirma: Sitchin: Ninurta's "divine black bird" was an aircraft.
a.entradas.ninurta.afirmaciones.0.replic: Ninurta is the warrior and agricultural god of Nippur, and his weapon Sharur is a personified weapon that talks with him in Lugal-e. The storm bird (the defeated Anzu) is a mythical emblem. The sources do not connect Ninurta with Egypt or with pyramids.
a.entradas.ninurta.afirmaciones.0.fuente: J. van Dijk, LUGAL UD ME-LÁM-bi NIR-ĞÁL, 1983; Black and Green, 1992
a.entradas.ninurta.veredicto: Ninurta is a god of war and agricultural fertility; his conversion into a fighter pilot is Sitchin's reading.
a.entradas.igigi.titulo_alternativo: The Igigi, the astronauts in orbit
a.entradas.igigi.interpretacion: Sitchin distinguishes between the Anunnaki stationed on Earth and the Igigi, some 300 astronauts who remained in orbit or at a station on Mars, in charge of transporting gold to Nibiru. In his account, the Igigi marry human women (an echo of the "sons of God" of Genesis 6) and rebel over their working conditions.
a.entradas.igigi.afirmaciones.0.afirmaci: Sitchin: the Igigi were 300 astronauts in orbit or on Mars.
a.entradas.igigi.afirmaciones.0.replica: Igigi is an Akkadian term for the great gods of heaven, often paired with Anunnaki to refer to the gods as a whole. In Atrahasis the Igigi are the gods who labor and rebel. Some late texts count 300 gods of heaven and 600 of the earth, but these are cosmological figures, unrelated to Mars or to orbits.
a.entradas.igigi.afirmaciones.0.fuente_r: Lambert and Millard, 1969; Black and Green, 1992; Colavito, review of Ancient Aliens S6E03 (on Ancient Aliens' fiction of the Anunnaki on Mars)
a.entradas.igigi.veredicto: The Igigi are a category of gods in Mesopotamian theology; their role as an orbital crew is a narrative invention.
a.entradas.dilmun.titulo_alternativo: Dilmun/Tilmun, the land of the rockets
a.entradas.dilmun.interpretacion: In The Stairway to Heaven (1980), Sitchin distinguishes between Dilmun, the paradise of Enki and Ninhursag, and Tilmun, "the land of the missiles", which he places on the Sinai Peninsula as the site of the Anunnaki's post-Flood spaceport. Gilgamesh would have traveled there in search of immortality.
a.entradas.dilmun.afirmaciones.0.afirmac: Sitchin: Tilmun is Sinai, "the land of the missiles".
a.entradas.dilmun.afirmaciones.0.replica: Dilmun (also written Tilmun) is a trading region of the Persian Gulf identified with Bahrain and the eastern coast of Arabia thanks to inscriptions, seals and excavations (Qal'at al-Bahrain, on the UNESCO World Heritage List). The "missiles" etymology depends on the mistaken reading of MU and shem as rocket.
a.entradas.dilmun.afirmaciones.0.fuente_: H. Crawford, Dilmun and its Gulf Neighbours, 1998; Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com
a.entradas.dilmun.veredicto: Dilmun is a real place in the Persian Gulf, well documented by archaeology; its relocation to Sinai as a spaceport has no basis.
a.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.titulo: Enlil's lost testimony: the Anunnaki commander who voted to exterminate humanity
a.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.interp: In alternative popular history, above all in 2025 YouTube videos from anonymous channels such as "The Lost Vault" and "The Obsidian Vault", the "Lost Tablet of Enlil" is presented as a document "finally recovered" or "finally translated". In it Enlil, understood as the commander of extraterrestrial Anunnaki, would explain why he voted in the council of the gods to destroy humanity by means of the flood. His brother Enki/Ea would be the creator and protector of humans. This approach comes directly from Zecharia Sitchin, above all from "The 12th Planet" (1976) and "The Lost Book of Enki" (2002). In those books Enlil and Enki are two Anunnaki brothers from Nibiru at odds over the fate of humanity, and the flood is a catastrophe that Enlil deliberately allows. The videos present the tablet as "Enlil's version", the counterpart of the supposed book of Enki.
a.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.afirma: There is a tablet of Enlil, lost and recently recovered or translated, in which the god explains his decision to exterminate humanity.

No museum, catalog (CDLI, ORACC, ETCSL) or academic publication records such a tablet. The only "forgotten" tablet related to Enlil published in those years is Ni 12501 (Matuszak, Iraq 2024/2025), and it is not about destroying humanity: it tells of the rescue of the god Iškur, trapped in the Underworld, by a fox.
J. Matuszak, Iraq 86 (2024), pp. 79–108; UChicago News, August 15, 2025
This tablet reveals for the first time that Enlil voted against humanity.

Enlil's decision to annihilate humans with plagues and with the flood has long been known from Atrahasis (Old Babylonian) and from Tablet XI of Gilgamesh, published by George Smith in 1872. It is no new revelation, and in those texts Enlil is a god, not an extraterrestrial leader.
W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard, Atra-ḫasīs (1969); A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (2003)
Enlil and Enki were Anunnaki astronauts from Nibiru, and their tablets are historical chronicles.

This reading comes from Sitchin, whose translations Assyriology rejects. "The Lost Book of Enki" (2002) is an original work by Sitchin presented as a tablet dictated by Enki, but it does not correspond to any cuneiform text. In the sources, "Anunnaki" designates the great gods, and Nibiru is an astronomical point associated with Marduk, not an inhabited planet.
M. S. Heiser, critiques of Sitchin (sitchiniswrong.com); W. Horowitz, Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography (1998)
The "tablet" is the same Tablet of Destinies that Enlil kept: a stolen technological device.

The Tablet of Destinies is a mythical object that symbolizes authority over the cosmos. It appears in the myth of Anzu and in the Enuma Elish, and no text describes it as a machine. It is not an archaeological object that can be "lost" or "recovered".
A. Annus, The Standard Babylonian Epic of Anzu (SAACT 3, 2001)
a.entradas.tablilla-perdida-enlil.veredi: The "Lost Tablet of Enlil" is not documented in any ancient or academic source. It is a modern title from alternative popular history that recycles Atrahasis, the myth of Anzu and Sitchin's theses, capitalizing on the real news about tablet Ni 12501 in 2025.
a.cronologia.1919-0.evento: Charles Fort publishes The Book of the Damned, a compilation of anomalies that suggests visits by beings from other worlds.
a.cronologia.1928-0.evento: H. P. Lovecraft publishes "The Call of Cthulhu", with alien gods who came to Earth in the remote past; Jason Colavito places one of the roots of the ancient astronaut theory here.
a.cronologia.1960-0.evento: Louis Pauwels and Jacques Bergier publish Le Matin des magiciens, which popularizes in Europe the idea of lost ancient knowledge and of visitors from other worlds.
a.cronologia.1966-0.evento: I. S. Shklovskii and Carl Sagan publish Intelligent Life in the Universe, in which they cautiously propose studying the myth of Oannes as a possible memory of contact.
a.cronologia.1968-0.evento: Erich von Däniken publishes Erinnerungen an die Zukunft (Chariots of the Gods?), a worldwide success that turns the hypothesis into a mass phenomenon.
a.cronologia.1976-0.evento: Zecharia Sitchin publishes The 12th Planet and Robert K. G. Temple The Sirius Mystery: Mesopotamia becomes the center of the movement (Nibiru, Anunnaki, Oannes).
a.cronologia.1985-0.evento: Sitchin publishes The Wars of Gods and Men, with the thesis of a nuclear war among the Anunnaki around 2024 BC.
a.cronologia.1991-0.evento: The anthropologist Walter van Beek publishes his restudy of the Dogon in Current Anthropology: he finds no knowledge of Sirius B, the basis of Temple's thesis.
a.cronologia.1995-0.evento: Nancy Lieder launches ZetaTalk and announces the catastrophic passage of a "Planet X" for May 2003; her followers identify it with Sitchin's Nibiru.
a.cronologia.1996-0.evento: Alan F. Alford publishes Gods of the New Millennium, a bestseller in the United Kingdom based on Sitchin, which he himself would later revise and criticize.
a.cronologia.2003-0.evento: The date announced by Lieder passes without incident; the prediction is moved to 2012 and merged with the end of the Maya calendar. Around this time Michael S. Heiser publishes his analyses of the VA 243 seal and of Nibiru on sitchiniswrong.com.
a.cronologia.2005-0.evento: Michael Tellinger publishes Slave Species of god, Anton Parks Le Secret des Étoiles Sombres and Jason Colavito The Cult of Alien Gods, the first critical study of the movement's literary origins.
a.cronologia.2009-0.evento: History Channel airs the documentary Ancient Aliens, with Giorgio A. Tsoukalos, which becomes a series in 2010. That year Ronald H. Fritze publishes Invented Knowledge, with a detailed critique of Sitchin.
a.cronologia.2010-0.evento: Zecharia Sitchin dies in New York at the age of 90.
a.cronologia.2012-0.evento: NASA and David Morrison publicly debunk the Nibiru hoax and the end of the world in December 2012 (the "Beyond 2012" campaign); the date passes without incident.
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.0: Home-made translations and etymologies that do not follow the reference dictionaries (Chicago Assyrian Dictionary, Pennsylvania Sumerian Dictionary) or the grammar; for example, Anunnaki as "those who from heaven to Earth came", or MU and shem as "rocket" (Heiser; Fritze).
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.1: Iconography out of context: images from seals and reliefs taken without their inscription or comparison with the corpus. This is how the VA 243 seal is read as the Sun and its planets, and the apkallu's ritual bucket as a technological "handbag" (Heiser; Colavito).
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.2: Selective literalism: mythical and poetic language is taken as technical description (wings as spacecraft, personified weapons as bombs, heaven as a planet), while passages that do not fit are ignored, such as the human construction of the ziggurats in the Enuma Elish (W. I. Thompson; Colavito).
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.3: Mixing of periods and cultures: "the Sumerians" is used to refer to Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian texts separated by more than two millennia, and these are combined with the Bible, Egypt or the Dogon as if they were a single source (Colavito; Peter James).
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.4: Truncated or decontextualized quotations and the use of secondhand translations, sometimes loose literary adaptations, instead of philological editions (Fritze; Colavito on Von Däniken).
a.metodo.errores_frecuentes.5: Unfalsifiability and lack of specialist review: the works are not published in academic journals, criticism is attributed to orthodoxy or cover-ups, and failed predictions (Nibiru in 2003 and 2012) are reinterpreted instead of refuting the thesis (Morrison; Feder, Frauds, Myths, and Mysteries).
a.metodo.por_que_atrae: Critics agree that this movement responds to needs that academia does not satisfy on its own. It offers a grand unified narrative connecting scattered myths, the Bible and space science; it gives a transcendent meaning to human origins without resorting to traditional religion; and it flatters readers, who gain access to a "hidden truth" against experts presented as the guardians of a secret. Colavito shows that its roots lie in science fiction (Lovecraft and the pulp magazines) and in the UFO culture of the Cold War and the space race, which made the image of astronauts visiting other worlds seem plausible. Since 2009, the television format of Ancient Aliens, with rhetorical questions ("what if…?"), suggestive editing and interviewees presented as researchers, together with YouTube and social media, has multiplied its reach. Kenneth Feder and Ronald Fritze add that these theories often rest on the idea that ancient peoples could not have achieved their works on their own, a premise that detracts from the merit of the real cultures of Mesopotamia.
